scripts.opening:opening:
[intrigued] JAUNT: PULLMAN'S OTHER SON. A Monday afternoon in November 1904, outside the Pullman house at Eighteenth Street.

Four stops, around the Pullman house and down the street to the house of the family's son-in-law. George Pullman had twin sons, and the whole city knew their names. [short pause] [lowering voice] There was a third young man who claimed the name too. His mother told him on her deathbed who his father was, and he crossed an ocean to say so to Pullman's face. [short pause] The family called him a madman. [short pause] [wryly] The doctors kept saying he was sane.

[short pause] Start at the front of the house, where his story begins.
scripts.stop:mother: [quietly] 1729 Prairie, the Pullman house. Picture a German Army sergeant named Gustave Behring, 28 years old, at his mother's bedside. [short pause] [softly] Dying, she told him his real father was George M. Pullman. She had been a governess in Chicago "for a house on the west side", she said, and when she became pregnant, Pullman packed her off to Germany with $500. [short pause] [determined] Behring came to Chicago. He went to the Pullman building and was thrown out of Pullman's office. He was locked up for a time in an asylum, and arrested six more times lurking outside the building. [short pause] Four days before Pullman died, their conversation was recorded. [shouting] "BEHRING: You are my father! [angrily] PULLMAN: You are a crazy man!" [long pause] [quietly] The house will be razed in 1922. Walk round to the front steps.
scripts.stop:steps: [measured] The front steps. Pullman died in October 1897. [short pause] His family buried him under concrete and steel. [short pause] [dramatically] And "Less than 12 hours after the funeral, Behring showed up at the family's residence on Prairie Avenue, demanding to speak to Mrs. Harriett Pullman." [short pause] He never reached the door. On these steps he was met by Pullman's two sons, the twins, and by the family's lawyers. He was arrested again, and on 29 October 1897 an insanity expert examined him and pronounced him sane. [short pause] [wryly] Not a madman, then. [short pause] Just a man who would not go away. The Pullmans' housekeeper, Emma Scott, still answers this door. Walk round the corner to the glasshouse.
scripts.stop:ship: [quietly] The conservatory, the family's glass parlour. Behind this glass the Pullmans waited for the problem to leave. [short pause] In September 1898 it did: detectives walked Behring up the gangway of the Cunard liner Campania, bound for Bremen. [wryly] Europe could have him. [long pause] [ominous] But he came back. A man who has been told by his dying mother who his father was does not stay deported. And by 1901 the twins who had blocked the steps had troubles of their own. One of them, George Jr., would be dead by November. Florence Pullman's husband, Frank Lowden, was a lawyer. [short pause] So when Behring came back, he went to Lowden. Walk south down Prairie to the Lowden house.
scripts.stop:gun: [measured] 1912 Prairie, where Frank Lowden lives with Florence and their children. [short pause] Lowden is a careful man, but even careful men have bad afternoons. [dramatically] "on June 25, 1901, Behring was again arrested at the law offices of Frank Lowden (Florence Pullman's husband) demanding $5,000 in cash and $10,000 a month for 6 months." [short pause] [tense] Lowden's partner did not wait for the police to talk him out of it: "Judge Davis, Lowden's partner, held Behring at gunpoint until the police arrived". [short pause] The house will be razed in 1939. [short pause] [quietly] Watch Lowden come home this afternoon, and look back down the street before he goes in.
scripts.ending:name: [thoughtful] End of the walk. Gustave Behring was arrested, locked up, examined, found sane, put on a ship and arrested again, and as the papers told it his story ends at the point of a judge's gun. [long pause] [softly] "You are my father!" [short pause] "You are a crazy man!" [short pause] Those two sentences are all that is left of the only conversation the two men ever had, [short pause] [quietly] and you can decide for yourself which of them was telling the truth.
